Before you start

Students learn why BAC keeps rising after the last drink, how small a standard drink is, and the CUPS signs that mean call 911 every time. Bring a party cup and water for the pour demo, and never ask who drinks: some students don't for faith or family reasons, and some have a parent who drinks too much.

Every student in the room

Open by saying families, faiths and cultures see alcohol very differently, and that Theo's card (the student who doesn't drink) is a full, normal way to go to college.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students understand why blood alcohol keeps rising after the last drink, how small a standard drink is, what fake pills and mixing do, and exactly what to do when someone can't be woken. The lesson doesn't tell students whether to drink.

Materials

  • A clear party cup and a measuring cup or water bottle (for the pour demo)
  • Index cards, one per student
  • The student page link (last slide) to share afterward

Flow

  1. 2 minYour values, your choice
  2. 3 minThe curve that catches people
  3. 3 minPour a standard drink (demo)
  4. 3 minA myth, and fake pills
  5. 4 minKnow CUPS; what stops people calling (turn and talk)
  6. 5 minThree nights: Maya’s roommate, Theo, Leo, then close

Short on time (10-minute version)

The curve (3), know CUPS and Maya’s roommate (5), save the numbers (2).

Before you teach
Never ask who drinks.

Keep everything about the body, the math and helping others. Questions like "Who's been to a party?" put students in a bind.

Don't tell them what to choose.

The lesson says it up front: it won't decide for them. Seniors tune out a lecture fast; they listen to how BAC works and what to do for a friend.

Some students have a parent who drinks.

Alcohol can be painful at home. Keep examples to the invented cards, and if a student lingers after, check in. When Someone at Home Drinks or Uses is the student page for that.

Get the numbers right.

The Duke blackout figure (51%) is among students who had ever had alcohol, in one university survey. The 1,825 deaths figure is from 2005 and mostly traffic crashes. Say where numbers come from.

Good Samaritan laws vary.

Many states protect people who call for help in a drug overdose, and most colleges have medical amnesty for alcohol. Tell students to look up the law and policy where they'll be.

The Leo card is about assault risk.

Keep the frame on stepping in. The Red Zone lesson goes deeper; point to it rather than opening a long conversation here.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Faith and family values.

For many students, not drinking is a religious or family value. Say plainly that students who don't drink are often the most useful people at a party, and that it's a normal way to do college.

Bodies differ.

BAC depends on body size, sex, food, sleep and medications. Keep examples general and never single out a student's body.

Not every student is headed to campus parties.

Commuters, students living at home, gap-year students and students going to work or the military need CUPS and the pill facts too. These skills work anywhere.

Calling for help isn't the same for everyone.

Some students and families fear police or immigration consequences. Name campus safety, medical amnesty, Poison Control and Good Samaritan laws as part of the plan, and be honest that medical emergencies still mean 911.

Guys are helpers too.

Encourage everyone, boys included, to see themselves as the one who steps in. Avoid framing safety as a women's issue.

Family history.

Some students have family members with drinking problems or have lost someone to an overdose. Keep it about information and helping, never jokes about being drunk.

What the research says

Alcohol keeps moving from the stomach and small intestine into the blood, so BAC can keep climbing after the last drink and even after someone passes out. A US standard drink is 14 grams of alcohol: about 12 oz of beer, 5 oz of wine or 1.5 oz of liquor.

National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism

When college students free-poured drinks, they poured more than a standard drink every time, and the bigger the cup, the bigger the overpour.

White, Kraus and Swartzwelder, Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research, 2003

In a survey of 772 Duke undergraduates, 51% of students who had ever had alcohol reported at least one blackout, and 40% had one in the past year.

White, Jamieson-Drake and Swartzwelder, Journal of American College Health, 2002

Across many studies, college students consistently overestimate how much their peers drink and how fine their peers are with heavy drinking.

Borsari and Carey, Journal of Studies on Alcohol, 2003

College students who mixed alcohol with energy drinks reported more alcohol-related injuries and other serious consequences than students who drank alcohol alone.

O'Brien et al., Academic Emergency Medicine, 2008

About 1,825 US college students aged 18 to 24 died from alcohol-related unintentional injuries in 2005, most of them in traffic crashes.

Hingson, Zha and Weitzman, Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, 2009

Counterfeit pills pressed to look like Xanax, Percocet, oxycodone or Adderall often contain fentanyl or methamphetamine; in DEA testing, two in five fake pills with fentanyl held a potentially lethal dose. Naloxone (Narcan) has been sold over the counter since 2023.

US Drug Enforcement Administration, 2021 · US Food and Drug Administration, 2023
